newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia mourns Deng, assesses China's progress.
newsitem.headline: Russia mourns Deng, assesses China's progress.

text.p: Russian political leaders mourned on Thursday the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping -- but the occasion prompted uneasy comparisons between his course and that of post-communist Russia.

"It is with deep sorrow that I learned of the passing of China's outstanding state and political figure Deng Xiaoping, the herald and architect of reforms which prompted historic changes in that great and ancient state," President Boris Yeltsin said in a letter of condolence to Beijing.

The communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament observed a minute's silence in memory of the man whose policy of economic reform under strict communist control is the source of much soul-searching in a Russia where the arrival of democracy has been accompanied by a collapse in living standards.
"Deng was a whole epoch, a man who did unprecedented things," Sergei Ivanenko, deputy parliamentary leader of the liberal Yabloko party, told Reuters.
"But," he added, "His experience, which provided results in a country with a huge population and long-standing tradition of respect for authority, cannot be applied in Russia."
In contrast, leading communist Valentin Kuptsov said Deng's example showed to what extent Russia had taken the wrong road.
"The main mistake of our reformers was that they ignored all past experience," he said.
"They have thrown the country into uncertainty while the Chinese reforms were based on a stable political system."
But Kuptsov said that Russia, which faces mounting problems in relations with the West and is worried by NATO's plans to expand closer to its borders, was about to change.
"We have neglected the role of the state and we have weakened the state," said Kuptsov, whose party forms a strong, nationalistic opposition to Yeltsin.
"I think the administration is starting to realise this and we will change the situation, whoever is president," he added. "China's experience should be carefully examined."
Ivanenko said that though China was well ahead of Russia in economic reform, it was well behind Moscow in political achievements and that Beijing should brace for change.
"When I was in China in 1995 I suddenly realised that, in the political sense, I had returned to the Moscow of the late 1980s," he said.
"As I watched things developing I had a growing feeling that many episodes of the political struggle in Russia will inevitably repeat themselves in China."

Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov, a communist, said the Kremlin's pro-Western policy of the first post-Soviet years had not worked -- in contrast to Deng's commitment to putting China's interests first.

"We must understand that the West is investing generously in the Chinese economy, clearly unconcerned that this is a communist country but rather relying on the stability of its political situation," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

Deng's death at 92 also highlighted one more painful problem for Russia -- the state of health of its own leader, a relative stripling of 66, who had heart bypass surgery last November and is still recovering from a subsequent bout of pneumonia.
Opponents say Yeltsin, who has spent little time in the Kremlin since his reelection last July, is too weak to rule.
"Yeltsin can't be compared to Deng," Kuptsov said. "Deng was the pivot of the processes in China, which means he knew what he wanted to make of his country. With Yeltsin that's not the case."
